periods.activity_title: How Big Is a Lakh? Building Intuitive Scale

textbook_items_in_class.description: Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years? Also: if a person ate 3 varieties of rice every day, would they taste all lakh varieties in a 100-year lifetime? Standalone ? prompts building intuition about lakh.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000. How much more than one lakh is 1,06,000?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
homework.description: By how much did the population of Chintamani increase from 2011 to 2024?

time_bands.activity: Open with Eshwarappa's story: India once had a lakh varieties of rice. Students predict whether a lakh is large or small in everyday terms — hairs on a head, a cricket ground's crowd — and share their reasoning aloud.

Build the place-value pattern box on the board (3-digit → 4-digit → 5-digit → 6-digit boundary values) to establish 1,00,000 as the smallest six-digit number. Students read and write six- and seven-digit numbers in words using the Indian 3-2-2 comma pattern.

Figure it Out, section 1.1 p.2 ("Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years?....") — students choose their own value of y, compute, and compare with one lakh; class discusses whether a lifetime of rice tasting would cover all lakh varieties.

Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3 ("According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3 ("Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000....") — students compute differences from one lakh and write answers in words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the Indian comma pattern (3-2-2) with the international pattern (3-3-3); use the place-value box explicitly to anchor the position of the lakh's comma. Watch for students writing 'one lakh' as '100000' without the comma — reinforce the convention throughout. Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3 ("By how much did the population of Chintamani increase….") is assigned for reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Calculator Characters: Reasoning About Place-Value Decomposition

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Thoughtful Thousands (+1000 button): how many presses to show (a) 3,000 (b) 10,000 (c) 53,000 (d) 90,000 (e) 1 lakh (f) ? for 153 presses (g) how many thousands make one lakh?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tedious Tens (+10 button): how many presses to show (a) 500 (b) 780 (c) 1000 (d) 3700 (e) 10,000 (f) 1 lakh (g) ? for 435 presses.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Handy Hundreds (+100 button): how many presses to show (a)–(h) given targets; (i) hundreds to make ten thousand; (j) hundreds to make one lakh; (k) evaluate Handy Hundreds' claim about numbers Tedious Tens and Thoughtful Thousands cannot show.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the three calculator characters — Thoughtful Thousands (+1000), Tedious Tens (+10), Handy Hundreds (+100). Students discuss: which character would they prefer for reaching large targets quickly, and why?

Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5 ("Thoughtful Thousands (+1000 button): how many presses to show....") — students work in pairs, recording press counts; they articulate the pattern connecting press count with the thousands digit.

Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5 ("Tedious Tens (+10 button): how many presses to show....") — pairs compare totals for the same targets across both characters and begin to reason why button-press counts relate to place-value digit values.

Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5 ("Handy Hundreds (+100 button): how many presses to show....") including part (k) on Handy Hundreds' claim — class discusses which numbers each character can or cannot reach, surfacing the idea that reachability depends on divisibility by the button's value.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight to draw out is that some numbers (e.g., 780) cannot be reached by Thoughtful Thousands alone because 780 is not a multiple of 1000 — press the class to articulate the divisibility condition. Watch for students adding press counts across characters rather than finding the count for a single character. Figure it Out Q3 part (k) is the richest reasoning prompt and deserves unhurried class discussion.

periods.activity_title: Minimum Clicks and Place-Value Notation: Chitti and Sippy

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6
textbook_items_in_class.description: Creative Chitti: for each of 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813, write expressions for at least two different ways to obtain the number through button clicks.
Systematic Sippy: find how to get (a) 5072 and (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible. Write the expression.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: For 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813: find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks.
Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?
If you notice, the expressions for least button clicks also give the Indian place value notation of the numbers. Think about why this is so.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.2 p.6
homework.description: Find a different way to get 5072 beyond the two shown, and write an expression for it.
Creative Chitti challenges: (a) make the largest and smallest 3-digit numbers using exactly 30 button presses; (b) make 997 with a different number of clicks than 25.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6 ("Creative Chitti: for each of 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813, write expressions for at least two different ways....") — students work individually, then compare their different representations in pairs.

Figure it Out, section 1.2 p.7 ("Systematic Sippy: find how to get (a) 5072 and (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible....") followed by Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7 ("For 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813: find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks....") — students compete to minimise clicks and record their expressions.

Math Talk Q2, section 1.2 p.7 ("Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?...") — pairs share observations; teacher charts responses to surface the digit-sum connection.

Math Talk Q3, section 1.2 p.7 ("If you notice, the expressions for least button clicks also give the Indian place value notation of the numbers....") — class discusses why minimum clicks map directly onto place-value digits, consolidating the link between efficient decomposition and standard notation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that press counts depend on each button's step-size, students now apply that understanding to find minimum representations. The key connection — that the minimum-click expression is exactly the Indian place-value notation — can be missed if students focus only on arithmetic; ask them to write their expressions and compare with a place-value expansion side by side. Watch for students who add button-press counts from different characters for the same number rather than choosing one character per digit.

periods.activity_title: Crores, Millions, Arabs, Billions: Two Systems Side by Side

textbook_items_in_class.description: How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? How many zeros does a hundred thousand have? Standalone ? prompts on zero-counting for large named numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Read six numbers (4050678, 48121620, 20022002, 246813579, 345000543, 1020304050) and write their number names in both the Indian and American systems.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9
homework.description: Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions spanning crores, billions, and millions.

time_bands.activity: Build a side-by-side table on the board: Indian system (lakh, ten lakh, crore, ten crore, arab) versus American/International system (hundred thousand, million, ten million, hundred million, billion), noting the 3-2-2 versus 3-3-3 comma patterns. Students identify how many zeros each named value carries.

Figure it Out, section 1.3 p.8 ("How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? How many zeros does a hundred thousand have?...") — students compute and record, noticing where the two systems give different names to the same quantity.

Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9 ("Read six numbers (4050678, 48121620, 20022002, 246813579, 345000543, 1020304050) and write their number names in both the Indian and American systems....") — students work in pairs writing names in both systems, then cross-check with another pair.

Class debrief: students present one number each from the exercise, reading the name aloud in both systems. Teacher highlights which place-group boundaries differ between the two systems and where they coincide (thousands = thousands in both).

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is applying the 3-3-3 international grouping to Indian-system reading, yielding wrong names for numbers from 10 lakh onward; use the side-by-side table to keep both patterns visible throughout. Students who count zeros without anchoring to place-value position often misidentify a crore as having seven zeros — ask them to build the number by multiplying: 100 × 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,000. Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9 ("Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions….") is set for reinforcement.
materials: Printed or hand-drawn two-system place-value chart (one per pair)

periods.activity_title: Comparing Giants: Inequalities Across Indian and International Systems

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare and write '<', '>' or '=' for: (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: teacher writes one comparison on the board (e.g., 500 lakhs vs 5 million) and invites students to convert both to numerals before placing the inequality symbol. Class agrees on a procedure: convert all quantities to the same system, then compare digit counts and leading digits.

Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9 ("Compare and write '<', '>' or '=' for: (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion....") — students work individually, showing full conversion steps before placing the symbol.

Pairs compare answers and reconcile any disagreements by converting both quantities to numerals on paper and counting digits. Class focuses especially on parts (b) and (d) where the same numeral can be named differently in the two systems.
Teacher-led consolidation: draw attention to the pair 500 lakhs = 5 crore ≠ 5 million, reinforcing why naming-system awareness is essential before placing an inequality symbol.

periods.teacher_notes: The crore-versus-million confusion (10 million = 1 crore, not 1 million = 1 crore) is the most common error in part (b) and part (d); keep the two-system conversion table visible. Students who correctly convert but then compare only the number of digits (without checking the leading digit) may err on numbers with the same digit count — prompt them to compare the leftmost digit after confirming digit counts agree.

periods.activity_title: Nearest Neighbours: When Should We Round and Why?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding is okay, (d) exact numbers are needed.
Write the five nearest neighbours (nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore) for: (a) 3,87,69,957 and (b) 29,05,32,481.
I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000. What could the number be? How many such numbers are there?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the distinction between exact and approximate values using the sweet-shop scenario: ordering sweets requires rounding up (never run short), estimating pocket money requires rounding down. Establish the midpoint rule: digits 0–4 round down, 5–9 round up.

Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.10 ("Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding is okay, (d) exact numbers are needed....") — students generate real-life examples in pairs and share with the class, justifying each choice with a brief argument.

Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11 ("Write the five nearest neighbours (nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore) for: (a) 3,87,69,957 and (b) 29,05,32,481....") — students apply the midpoint rule at each place level, recording all five rounded values in a structured table.

Math Talk, section 1.4 p.11 ("I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000. What could the number be?...") — students reason about the range of values that round to 5,00,00,000 at every scale, then discuss how many such numbers there are.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently round each place independently without anchoring to the original number, leading to contradictory rounded values; insist they return to the original numeral for each of the five rounding operations. The Math Talk item is deceptively rich — the answer requires intersecting five rounding intervals, which surfaces a genuine reasoning challenge; allow students to express their thinking before revealing the range. Watch for confusion between 'round to the nearest lakh' and 'round to the nearest ten lakh'.
materials: Plain paper for structured rounding tables

periods.activity_title: Estimation in Action: Sums, Differences, and City Populations

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682: evaluate Roxie's and Estu's estimates; determine if sum exceeds 8,50,000; determine if sum exceeds 8,83,128; compute exact value.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate 14,63,128 − 4,90,020: evaluate Roxie's and Estu's estimates; determine if difference exceeds 9,50,000; determine if difference exceeds 9,63,128; compute exact value.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: What is your general observation about this data?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Populations of Cities: How much is Pune's population in 2011? By approximately how much has it increased compared to 2001?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.4 p.13
homework.description: Populations of Cities: Which city's population increased the most between 2001 and 2011?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.4 p.13
homework.description: Populations of Cities: Are there cities whose population has almost doubled? Which are they?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11 ("Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682: evaluate Roxie's and Estu's estimates....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.4 p.11 ("Estimate 14,63,128 − 4,90,020: evaluate Roxie's and Estu's estimates....") — students compute estimates using each child's method, then answer the threshold questions before computing exact values.

Class debrief on the two estimation problems: teacher compares Roxie's and Estu's strategies, asking students which estimates are over- or under-estimates and why, reinforcing that rounding direction affects whether an estimate exceeds a threshold.

Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.13 ("Populations of Cities: What is your general observation about this data?...") and Figure it Out Q3, section 1.4 p.13 ("Populations of Cities: How much is Pune's population in 2011? By approximately how much has it increased?...") — students read the population table, make general observations, and compute Pune's approximate increase using rounding.

Brief class share: two or three students read their general observation about the city-population data (Q1), and the class checks Pune's approximate increase together, connecting the rounding procedure to the population context.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised the nearest-neighbour rounding procedure, students now use rounding as a tool for decision-making — the threshold questions (does the sum exceed 8,50,000?) are the key application. A common slip is rounding both addends down and then claiming the sum must exceed a threshold; remind students that rounding down produces an underestimate, which cannot confirm a lower bound. Figure it Out Q4 and Q5 on city populations are set for independent reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Why Do Roxie's and Estu's Shortcuts Work? Justifying Multiplication Methods

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.

Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie's claim that the product of two 2-digit numbers is always 3- or 4-digit. Is there a better way than exhaustive checking?
Can multiplying a 3-digit number with another 3-digit number give a 4-digit number? Can multiplying a 4-digit number with a 2-digit number give a 5-digit number?

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example (Roxie's method), section 1.5 p.13 ("Roxie evaluates 116 × 5 by rewriting 5 as 10/2....") and Example (Estu's method), section 1.5 p.14 ("Estu evaluates 824 × 25 by rewriting 25 as 100/4....") as demonstrations, reading them from the textbook together as a class.

Math Talk, section 1.5 p.14 ("Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10....") — students write a justification using the identity 5 = 10 ÷ 2 and the associativity of multiplication, then share in pairs before a class discussion.

Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 ("Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie's claim that the product of two 2-digit numbers is always 3- or 4-digit....") — students examine several products, propose a boundary-case argument using the smallest and largest two-digit numbers, and check whether the same logic explains the claim without exhaustive testing.

Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 ("Can multiplying a 3-digit number with another 3-digit number give a 4-digit number?...") — students apply boundary-case reasoning to new factor-size combinations and articulate the general rule emerging from their examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes accept Roxie's shortcut as a trick without understanding its basis; insist that the Math Talk justification be written using multiplication-and-division meaning (5 = 10/2, so n × 5 = n × 10/2 = (n/2) × 10) before moving to digit-count arguments. The boundary-case method — testing the smallest-times-smallest and largest-times-largest products — is a powerful and transferable technique; name it explicitly so students can reuse it. Watch for students who claim a 3-digit × 3-digit product must always be 6-digit, ignoring the (2d−1)-digit lower bound.

periods.activity_title: Quick Calculations and Pattern Tables: Applying Multiplication Shortcuts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14
Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.14

textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate four sets of pattern multiplications (11×11, 111×111 …; 66×61, 666×661 …; 3×5, 33×35 …; 101×101, 102×102 …) and extend each pattern.
Extend the digit-product pattern table: fill in results for 5-digit × 5-digit, 8-digit × 3-digit, and 12-digit × 13-digit.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14 ("Find quick ways to calculate: (a) 2 × 1768 × 50; (b) 72 × 125 [Hint: 125 = 1000/8]; (c) 125 × 40 × 8 × 25....") — students select and name the shortcut (Roxie's, Estu's, or a combination) they apply to each part, showing the rewritten form before computing.

Figure it Out Q2, section 1.5 p.14 ("Calculate these products quickly: (a) 25 × 12; (b) 25 × 240; (c) 250 × 120; (d) 2500 × 12; (e) ___×___= 120000000....") — students observe the scaling pattern across parts (a)–(d) and use it to propose a valid pair of factors for part (e).

Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.14 ("Evaluate four sets of pattern multiplications (11×11, 111×111 …; 66×61, 666×661 …; 3×5, 33×35 …; 101×101, 102×102 …) and extend each pattern....") — students compute the first two products in each set, identify the pattern, and write the next two terms.

Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 ("Extend the digit-product pattern table: fill in results for 5-digit × 5-digit, 8-digit × 3-digit, and 12-digit × 13-digit....") — students apply the (2d−1)- or 2d-digit boundary rule to complete the table, connecting the pattern-discovery work back to the boundary-case reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who compute part (e) of Figure it Out Q2 by trial and error rather than using the scaling relationship from parts (a)–(d) are missing the point; ask them to articulate the pattern before guessing a factor pair. In the pattern-multiplication sets, students often spot the surface pattern (palindromic products, incremental sequences) without being able to say why it holds — asking 'what changes and what stays the same across each row?' can deepen the observation. Watch for arithmetic slips when applying the 125 = 1000/8 hint in Q1(b).

periods.activity_title: Fascinating Facts and Moon Journeys: Large-Number Estimation in Context

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fascinating Facts — compute products/quotients to uncover hidden facts: (a) 1250 × 380 = kīrtanas by Purandaradāsa; (b) 2100 × 70,000 = approximate Earth-Sun distance in km; (c) 6400 × 62,500 = Amazon river discharge litres/second; (d) 13,95,000 ÷ 150 = longest single-train journey km; (e) 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700 = blue whale weight kg; (f) 52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 = global plastic waste weight in tonnes. Read results in both naming systems.
Could Mumbai's entire population (1 crore 24 lakh) fit into 1 lakh buses (50 people each)? Could it fit into 5000 Titanic ships (2500 passengers each)?
If Roxie travels 100 km/day, can she reach the Moon (3,84,400 km) in 10 years? Find out if you can reach the Sun in a lifetime travelling 1000 km/day.

homework.description: Make necessary assumptions and answer: (a) Can you lift 1 lakh sheets of paper (5 g each)? (b) If 250 babies born per minute, will 1 million be born in a day? (c) Can you count 1 million coins in a day at 1 coin/second?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.16 ("Fascinating Facts — compute products/quotients to uncover hidden facts: (a) 1250 × 380 = kīrtanas by Purandaradāsa; (b) 2100 × 70,000 = approximate Earth-Sun distance in km....") — students work through all six computations in pairs, applying multiplication shortcuts where applicable and reading each result in both the Indian and American naming systems.

Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.18 ("Could Mumbai's entire population (1 crore 24 lakh) fit into 1 lakh buses (50 people each)?...") — students set up the division, compute the capacity, and compare it with the population to give a reasoned yes/no answer; they then repeat for the Titanic scenario.

Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.19 ("If Roxie travels 100 km/day, can she reach the Moon (3,84,400 km) in 10 years?...") — students estimate total travel days in 10 years, compute total distance, and compare with 3,84,400 km; they then reframe the calculation for the Sun, adjusting to a lifetime at 1000 km/day.

Class reflection: students share one surprising result from the Fascinating Facts computations and name which naming system (Indian or American) they find more natural for that result, consolidating the cross-system reading skill.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often perform the arithmetic correctly but fail to state a conclusion (yes/no with a comparison); insist that every problem ends with an explicit comparison between their computed result and the given benchmark. In the Moon and Sun distance problems, watch for students who compute days without converting 10 years to days — ask them to state their conversion explicitly before dividing. Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.19 (assumption-based problems) is set for reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Four Problems, One Chapter: Large Numbers Put to Work
periods.teacher_notes: Pose all four problems together by writing them on the board. Students work individually with full working — do not accept answers without written steps. Groups of three then compare working; any disagreement must be reconstructed step by step, not resolved by majority vote. Four volunteers present, one per problem; after each presentation the class names aloud the chapter method the solution used. Watch for: Problem 1 — students forgetting to count the digit-sum as the minimum clicks, or losing track of the Indian comma grouping when writing the answer in words; Problem 2 — rounding to the wrong place, or rounding both numbers in the same direction when checking whether the sum crosses a boundary; Problem 3 — applying Estu's method only to the first factor and not pausing to check whether the second also admits a shortcut; Problem 4 — treating the 7-digit × 2-digit product as definitely 8-digit without checking the boundary case (smallest 7-digit × smallest 2-digit vs. largest 7-digit × largest 2-digit).

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A number has the digits 4, 0, 7, 2, 6, 1, 3 in that order from left to right, making a 7-digit number. Write it in the Indian place-value system with commas, give its name in the Indian system, and state the smallest number of calculator button-presses (using +1000, +100, and +10 buttons) needed to reach it. | The number is 40,72,613. Indian name: Forty lakh seventy-two thousand six hundred and thirteen. Minimum button-presses = digit sum = 4+0+7+2+6+1+3 = 23. (Each digit tells how many times its place-value button is pressed; minimum because any other decomposition uses more presses in total.)
2 | Round 36,84,729 to its nearest ten lakh and its nearest lakh. Then decide, without computing the exact sum, whether 36,84,729 + 28,43,150 is more than 65,00,000 or less. Justify your answer. | Nearest ten lakh: 40,00,000 (since 6,84,729 > 5,00,000, round up). Nearest lakh: 37,00,000 (since 84,729 > 50,000, round up). For the sum: round each number down to the nearest ten lakh — 30,00,000 + 20,00,000 = 50,00,000; round each up — 40,00,000 + 30,00,000 = 70,00,000. Both addends are closer to 37,00,000 and 28,00,000; their sum 36,84,729 + 28,43,150 = 65,27,879, which exceeds 65,00,000. A sufficient justification without exact arithmetic: rounding both down to the nearest lakh gives 36,84,000 + 28,43,000 = 65,27,000 > 65,00,000, so the exact sum must also exceed 65,00,000.
3 | A school has 25 rows of seats in its hall, each row holding 480 seats. Using a multiplication shortcut, find the total number of seats. Then multiply that total by 5 using a second shortcut. Show your reasoning for both steps. | Step 1 — multiply by 25: 25 = 100 ÷ 4, so 480 × 25 = 480 × 100 ÷ 4 = 48,000 ÷ 4 = 12,000 seats. (Estu's method.) Step 2 — multiply 12,000 by 5: 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so 12,000 × 5 = 12,000 ÷ 2 × 10 = 6,000 × 10 = 60,000. (Roxie's method.) Total after scaling: 60,000.
4 | A 7-digit number is multiplied by a 2-digit number. How many digits can the product have? Give the smallest possible digit-count and the largest possible digit-count, with one example for each. | Smallest product: fewest digits occur when both factors are as small as possible. Smallest 7-digit number = 10,00,000; smallest 2-digit number = 10. Product = 10,00,00,000, which is 9 digits. Largest product: largest 7-digit = 99,99,999; largest 2-digit = 99. Product = 99,99,999 × 99 < 1,00,00,000 × 100 = 1,00,00,00,000 (10 digits), and 99,99,999 × 99 = 98,99,99,901, which is 10 digits. So the product is always either 8 digits — wait, check: 10,00,000 × 10 = 10,00,00,000 is already 9 digits. Try the true minimum: 10,00,000 × 10 = 10,00,00,000 (9 digits). Can we get 8 digits? The product would need to be less than 10,00,00,000, meaning less than 10,00,000 × 10 — but 10,00,000 is the smallest 7-digit number and 10 is the smallest 2-digit number, so no product of a 7-digit and a 2-digit number can be less than 10,00,00,000. The product therefore has either 9 digits (e.g., 10,00,000 × 10 = 10,00,00,000) or 10 digits (e.g., 99,99,999 × 99 = 98,99,99,901). It is always 9 or 10 digits.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board and reads each aloud. Students read them through once, ask only clarifying questions about wording (not method), and begin individual work.

Individual work: every student attempts all four problems in their notebook, writing full working for each. The teacher circulates silently, noting which problems surface the most hesitation, and does not intervene with method hints.

Groups of three compare answers. Where answers disagree, the group reconstructs both solutions step by step and identifies the point of divergence. The teacher listens to one or two groups and, if a group has resolved a disagreement incorrectly, asks them to read their steps aloud — a wrong step usually becomes visible when stated.

Four volunteers present one problem each at the board, showing steps. After each presentation the class names the chapter method used: Problem 1 — Indian place-value notation and digit-sum as minimum button-presses; Problem 2 — rounding to nearest neighbour and using rounded values to bound an exact sum; Problem 3 — Estu's method (×25) then Roxie's method (×5); Problem 4 — boundary-case reasoning about digit-count in a product. The teacher accepts a name only when the class can state which step in the solution it describes.

Teacher states the chapter's one idea aloud: every large number has an exact place in the base-ten system, and that place tells us how to name it, round it, compute with it, and bound the size of results — which is why all four problems yielded to the same set of methods.

items.prompt: Which of the following is equal to one lakh?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1,00,000 — the smallest six-digit number in the Indian place-value system, read as 'One Lakh'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the place-value pattern box: 3-digit boundary is 100, 4-digit is 1000, 5-digit is 10,000, 6-digit is 1,00,000 = one lakh.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has identified ten thousand (five-digit boundary) rather than one lakh, likely confusing the position of the lakh place.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has written ten lakh (seven digits) rather than one lakh, shifting the comma group one step too far.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has written one crore (eight digits), confusing lakh with crore in the Indian naming hierarchy.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to consult the place-value pattern box built in class and count digits before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the number name and numeral for ten lakh and one crore as well, distinguishing all three.

items.prompt: How many zeros does one crore have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build from the definition: 1 crore = 100 × 1 lakh = 100 × 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,000; count the zeros.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused one crore with one lakh (5 zeros), staying one naming step below.

items.prompt: A calculator has only a '+1000' button. Priya says she can display 47,000 using exactly 47 presses. Ravi says she needs exactly 47 presses. Tariq says she needs only 47 presses but cannot display 47,500 at all using this button alone. Who is correct about 47,000, and why? Also explain why 47,500 cannot be displayed using only the +1000 button.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both Priya and Ravi are correct about 47,000: 47 × 1000 = 47,000, so exactly 47 presses are needed. 47,500 cannot be displayed because 47,500 is not a multiple of 1000 (47,500 ÷ 1000 = 47.5, which is not a whole number), and each press adds exactly 1000, so only multiples of 1000 are reachable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A number is reachable by the +1000 button alone if and only if it is a multiple of 1000; press count equals the number divided by 1000.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to try dividing 47,000 by 1000 and then 47,500 by 1000, and ask what they notice about the remainder.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state which numbers between 47,000 and 48,000 can be displayed using only the +1000 button, and give a general rule for any target number.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper needs to pack exactly 1,48,763 sweets into gift boxes that hold 100 sweets each. Should she round 1,48,763 to the nearest hundred and use that many sweets, or use the exact number? Justify your answer by explaining when rounding up, rounding down, or using exact values is the right choice.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The shopkeeper should use the exact number 1,48,763. Rounding to the nearest hundred gives 1,48,800, which means buying 37 extra sweets unnecessarily; rounding down to 1,48,700 means she is short by 63 sweets and some boxes go unfilled. For packing problems where a specific quantity is required, exact values are appropriate. Rounding up is suitable when you must not run short (e.g., ordering extra boxes as a buffer), and rounding down when you must not exceed a limit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Exact values are needed when a precise count is required; rounding up avoids shortage; rounding down avoids excess — choose based on the consequence of error.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first describe one situation each where running short is a problem and where having extra is a problem, then apply that reasoning to sweets.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to describe a situation where rounding down is the safer choice even if it means having fewer items than needed, and justify their reasoning.

exercise.description: Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding is okay, (d) exact numbers are needed.

items.prompt: Meena says: 'Multiplying any number by 25 gives the same result as multiplying it by 100 and then dividing by 4.' Using the meaning of multiplication and division, write a justification explaining why Meena's claim is correct. Then state whether the product of two 3-digit numbers can ever be a 5-digit number, giving a boundary-case argument.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meena is correct because 25 = 100 ÷ 4, so n × 25 = n × (100 ÷ 4) = (n × 100) ÷ 4. Multiplying by 100 shifts the number two places left, and dividing by 4 reduces it, giving the same result as multiplying by 25 directly. For the digit-count argument: the smallest 3-digit number is 100 and the smallest product is 100 × 100 = 10,000 (a 5-digit number); the largest is 999 × 999 = 998,001 (a 6-digit number). So the product of two 3-digit numbers is always either 5-digit or 6-digit — it can indeed be 5-digit (e.g., 100 × 100 = 10,000).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rewrite 25 = 100/4 so n × 25 = (n × 100)/4; then use boundary cases (smallest × smallest, largest × largest) to determine digit-count range.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first verify Meena's claim with a specific number (e.g., 8 × 25 = 200 and 8 × 100 ÷ 4 = 200), then try to express 25 as a fraction of 100.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to extend the argument: what are the possible digit counts for the product of a 4-digit number and a 3-digit number, and why?

exercise.description: Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.

items.prompt: A calculator has three buttons: +10,000; +1,000; and +100. Write an expression using these buttons to display 63,400. How many button presses does your expression use in total? Is this the minimum possible? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 63,400 = 6 × 10,000 + 3 × 1,000 + 4 × 100. Expression: 6(+10,000) + 3(+1,000) + 4(+100). Total presses = 6 + 3 + 4 = 13. This is the minimum because using a smaller button where a larger one fits increases the press count (e.g., replacing one +10,000 with ten +1,000 presses adds 9 extra clicks), and the digit-sum of the place-value representation gives the fewest total presses.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose the number using the largest available button first (place-value from left), then sum the coefficients for the minimum press count.

inclusivity.support: Suggest writing 63,400 in expanded form (60,000 + 3,000 + 400) first, then matching each part to the available button.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a second expression for 63,400 that uses more button presses, write it out, and calculate the new total, explaining why it is not the minimum.

items.prompt: A wildlife reserve has 3,200 elephants. Each elephant drinks approximately 190 litres of water per day. Calculate the total water consumed by all elephants in one day. Write your answer in both the Indian naming system and the American naming system.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3,200 × 190 = 3,200 × 19 × 10 = 60,800 × 10 = 6,08,000 litres. Indian system: Six lakh eight thousand litres. American system: 608,000 = Six hundred and eight thousand litres.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 3200 × 190 by breaking 190 = 19 × 10: compute 3200 × 19 = 60,800 then multiply by 10; write the result in both naming systems using their respective comma conventions.

items.prompt: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0 exactly once each, write the largest possible 10-digit number that is a multiple of 5. Explain how you decided which digit to place in each position.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A multiple of 5 must end in 0 or 5. To maximise the number, place the largest available digits from left to right. Since 0 is smaller than 5, ending in 5 and placing 0 as high as possible (second position from the right) gives a larger result than ending in 0. Largest multiple of 5 ending in 5: arrange remaining digits 9,8,7,6,4,3,2,1,0 from left and place 0 as far right as possible before the 5. Optimal arrangement: 9,8,7,6,4,3,2,1,0,5 → 9,876,432,105 — but 0 cannot be the leading digit. Place 0 in the second-to-last position: 9876431205. Verify: using digits 0–9 once, largest multiple of 5 = 9,876,431,205 (ends in 5, with 0 placed one from the right to minimise its positional loss). Indian system: Nine arab eighty-seven crore sixty-four lakh thirty-one thousand two hundred and five.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix the units digit as 5 (ending in 5 gives a larger number than ending in 0 when 0 must appear somewhere); place remaining digits in descending order left to right, inserting 0 as far right as possible without leading.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that a multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5, then ask them to write the digits 0–9 in descending order and decide which ending digit gives the larger number.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also write the smallest 10-digit even number using digits 0–9 exactly once and compare both results in the Indian naming system.
